payload.throughline: Classify attitude versus action, locate the actor or institutional mechanism producing an outcome, and explain how unequal control of resources, status, and class position can amplify or stabilize discrimination.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: identify whether a vignette describes an attitude, an observable action, or an organizational rule.
Goal: separate prejudice from discrimination and separate individual action from institutional mechanisms.
The classification is sociological and construct-level. It does not determine legal liability, moral blame, or which policy should be adopted.

Prejudice is an evaluative attitude or affective orientation toward a social group. A stereotype is a generalized cognitive belief about a group. Discrimination is behavior or differential treatment tied to group membership.

Individual discrimination is enacted by a person or small set of people through their choices. Institutional discrimination is produced through an organization's rules, routines, criteria, or patterned practices that distribute treatment or opportunity unequally.

Intent and mechanism are separate questions. An institutional process can reproduce unequal treatment even when a vignette supplies no evidence that every participant holds an explicit prejudicial attitude.
Use a two-axis matrix. Axis 1: internal attitude/belief versus observable treatment. Axis 2, only for treatment: person-level choice versus rule/routine-level mechanism.

If a manager privately dislikes a group but applies the same procedure to every applicant, the evidence directly supports prejudice but not a discriminatory action. If the manager rejects an applicant because of group membership, that is individual discrimination. If a standardized organizational rule systematically excludes the group, the mechanism is institutional.

Worked example: a club member expresses a negative group attitude, one interviewer denies an otherwise eligible applicant because of group identity, and an organization uses a recurring eligibility rule that screens out the same group. These map to prejudice, individual discrimination, and institutional discrimination, respectively.
Guided practice: underline the observed evidence, then classify attitude/action before selecting individual/institutional.
Less help: distinguish one decision-maker's choice from a standing organizational routine.
On your own: avoid inferring a stable attitude when only an institutional outcome is observed.
Boundary: an unequal group outcome alone does not identify the exact mechanism; a classification needs evidence about decisions, rules, or routines.
Non-example: labeling a private attitude as institutional discrimination skips both the action requirement and the institutional mechanism.
Near exit: classify a fresh vignette with attitude, action, and mechanism cues separated.
Changed exit: infer which additional observation would distinguish individual from institutional discrimination in an ambiguous outcome pattern.
Repair the near-use function: quote the observable in neutral terms, choose attitude or action, and only then ask who or what mechanism enacted the action.
Fresh re-entry: classify a new workplace vignette with untouched actors and rule structure.
Repair the changed-task function: when outcome data are ambiguous, request mechanism evidence—one actor's choice versus a recurring formal or informal organizational practice.
Fresh re-entry: select the discriminating observation in a new educational setting.
Recap: prejudice is attitude, discrimination is action, individual discrimination is person-enacted, and institutional discrimination operates through organizational rules or routines.
Starting check: identify whether a vignette supplies control over decisions, socially recognized status, or class-linked resource access.
Goal: explain a mechanism linking power, prestige, or class position to the enactment or institutionalization of discrimination.
This lesson describes mechanisms. It does not prescribe policy, decide legal standards, or treat social categories as fixed traits of individuals.
Power is the capacity to influence decisions, control resources, or shape consequences. It enables an attitude or preference to affect other people's opportunities when the actor controls a gate.
Prestige is socially recognized status or honor. It can make some voices more credible, amplify influence over norms, or provide access to decision-makers even without direct formal authority.

Class position is linked to material resources, networks, education, and institutional access. These resources can shape who enters decision spaces, withstands exclusion, or transmits advantage. When unequal allocation becomes a recurring rule or routine, discrimination is institutionalized.

Use a causal chain: social position or status → control/access/credibility → gatekeeping decision or routine → differential treatment or opportunity. Require evidence for each arrow; do not infer the chain from outcome alone.

If an executive controls hiring criteria, the executive's power provides a decision channel. If a high-prestige professional group's recommendations are accepted without scrutiny, prestige provides influence. If class-linked networks determine who hears about openings, class resources shape access. I still need the group-linked differential action to classify discrimination.

Worked example: a professional association's high-prestige members define an informal referral norm; leadership turns that norm into a recurring hiring routine; applicants outside class-linked networks receive fewer opportunities. Prestige amplifies credibility, power converts the norm into procedure, and class-linked network access distributes the consequence.
Guided practice: label the enabling resource, the gate it affects, and the resulting differential action.
Less help: distinguish prestige-based influence from formal decision power.
On your own: avoid claiming a causal mechanism when a vignette provides only a group disparity.
Boundary: power, prestige, and class can facilitate discrimination, but none proves discrimination without evidence of group-linked differential action or allocation.
Non-example: equating high income with prejudice mistakes a class-related resource for an attitude.
Near exit: trace a fresh resource-to-gate-to-action mechanism and identify the enabling dimension.
Changed exit: identify which modeled causal change removes the institutional channel while leaving an individual's private attitude unmeasured.
Repair the near-use function: name the controlled resource or status, the decision gate, and the observable differential allocation in three separate clauses.
Fresh re-entry: explain a new prestige-and-power mechanism in a different organization.

Repair the changed-task function: institutionalization occurs when a discretionary pattern is encoded in a repeatable rule or routine; a diagram that removes that routine changes the institutional channel without proving attitude change.
Fresh re-entry: analyze a new causal diagram with a different rule-formation step.
Recap: power controls decisions and resources, prestige amplifies influence, class shapes resources and access, and recurring organizational routines can stabilize differential treatment.
